case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: Accolade needed the copy to achieve interoperability, a purpose the court treated as legitimate and narrow. Whether producing a competing creative work is the same kind of purpose is exactly what is now contested.
case.holding: Copying a program in full in order to study it is fair use when that copying is the only way to reach the unprotected functional elements inside and there is a legitimate reason to reach them.
case.case_name: Sega Enterprises Ltd. v. Accolade, Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: This is the intermediate copying line: the copy made along the way is judged by what it was for, not by the fact that it was complete. Training pipelines rely on it because ingestion necessarily makes copies before any output exists.

reading.body:
Sega v. Accolade, a 1992 case holding that copying a program in full to study its unprotected functional elements is fair use, is cited across 79 active lawsuits, more than any other precedent in this collection, in defense of AI training practices.

Its reach that wide means this single 1992 video-game reverse-engineering case has become one of the load-bearing precedents for the entire AI training-data legal defense, on the theory that ingestion necessarily makes copies before any output exists, the same intermediate-copying logic the original case applied to interoperability. The case's own limit is precise. The original copying was for interoperability specifically, and whether producing a competing creative work counts as the same kind of legitimate purpose is exactly what is now being litigated.

The data does not say how many of the 79 citing cases have reached a ruling on this specific argument, only that the precedent is currently invoked in all of them.
